clue.text: Day nursery for Indian outside the church

indicators.note: outside says the first word's letters wrap round the second's

parts.note: the Cree are a Native American people, an Indian in crossword usage
CH is the standard abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: Someone picks a day nursery for an Indian child just beyond the church.
explanation.walkthrough: The Indian is from North America: the Cree are a First Nations people, a staple of crossword Indians.
explanation.definitionFit: A crèche is a place where small children are minded during the day while their parents work.

clue.text: Man wants no end of Greek bread

indicators.note: to want something is to lack it, and lacking an end means the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a chap is a man
Attic means of Attica, the region round Athens, hence Greek

explanation.surface: A man goes without the last of the Greek bread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek bread' wants to be read together as pitta, but the bread is the definition and Greek is ATTIC, cut short to ATTI.
explanation.definitionFit: Chapatti is an unleavened flatbread of India, cooked on a griddle.

clue.text: Pendant let slip — Cockney to catch first

indicators.note: first tells us this piece is placed ahead of the other one

parts.note: to catch a sound is to hear it, and a Cockney drops the H
to let something slip from your hand is to drop it

explanation.surface: Someone let a pendant slip, and a Cockney must catch it before it falls.
explanation.walkthrough: A Cockney is a Londoner from the East End, whose accent famously drops the H, so 'hear' becomes EAR.
explanation.definitionFit: An eardrop is an earring with a hanging ornament, a pendant worn on the ear.

clue.text: In class, under 50 per cent maybe Anglo-Indian

definitions.note: a dated and now offensive term for a person of mixed descent

indicators.note: in a down entry, under places this piece below the following one

parts.note: fifty per cent is a half
a caste is a hereditary social class, especially in India

explanation.surface: In a classroom, someone scores under half marks, perhaps a pupil of Anglo-Indian descent.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'under' puts CASTE below HALF; 'maybe' warns that the definition is one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The term, now regarded as offensive, was historically used for people of mixed European and Indian parentage.

clue.text: One-sided pike

definitions.meaning: first meaning: biased, taking one faction's part
second meaning: a long-shafted spear with a broad blade, a medieval weapon

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pike' suggests the fish, but here it is the weapon; the two words share no surface link.
explanation.definitionFit: Partisan works as an adjective for prejudiced support and as a noun for a type of halberd-like polearm.

clue.text: Finished article store exhibits in every possible place

parts.note: when something is all over, it is finished
the definite article
a store is a shop

explanation.surface: A shop displays its finished goods in every available spot.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means scattered everywhere, in a disorganised way.

clue.text: Mathematician's premature end in Italian city

indicators.note: an end that comes too soon cuts the word short before its last letter

parts.note: Alan Turing, the British mathematician and codebreaker

explanation.surface: A mathematician died young in an Italian city.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is grimly apt, since Turing himself died early; here his name simply loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Turin is the capital of the Piedmont region in north-west Italy.

clue.text: Surprisingly dull dress for Zuleika Dobson?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: dark and drab in colour
second meaning: the formal dark academic dress worn at Oxford, where Max Beerbohm's novel is set

explanation.surface: Zuleika Dobson, a dazzling beauty, is oddly turned out in drab clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Surprisingly' looks like an anagram signal but is not; it is surprising because Beerbohm's heroine is a femme fatale who sets all Oxford alight.
explanation.definitionFit: Subfusc means dusky or sombre, and is also the dark clothing required at Oxford examinations and ceremonies.

clue.text: New, perfect fruitcake

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new
perfect in the sense of complete, as in a perfect stranger

explanation.surface: A baker presents a new and flawless fruitcake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruitcake' looks like the cake, but it is slang for an eccentric or mad person.
explanation.definitionFit: Nutter and fruitcake are both informal words for a crazy person.

clue.text: The foundling's birthplace?

parts.note: surface reading: the unknown place where an abandoned child was born, perhaps a hospital or workhouse
setter's reading: the plant under which, children are told in jest, new babies are found

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the old nursery fib told to children asking where babies come from: they are found in the garden under a fruit bush.
explanation.definitionFit: By that tale a baby is literally found there, so it is the birthplace of a foundling.

clue.text: One taken in after the first quarter

definitions.text: One taken in after the first quarter

parts.words: One taken in after the first quarter
parts.note: surface reading: someone admitted somewhere after the opening fifteen minutes or first term

parts.words: One taken in after the first quarter
parts.note: setter's reading: a person tricked on the first day of the year's second quarter

explanation.walkthrough: The year's first quarter is January to March, so the day after it ends is 1 April; 'taken in' means fooled, not admitted.
explanation.definitionFit: An April fool is the victim of a prank played on the first of April, the opening day of the second quarter.

clue.text: Quash return of Murphy's supporter

indicators.note: a return sends something back the way it came, so the word is read from its end

parts.note: murphy is slang for a potato, and the potato plant grows from and is sustained by an underground tuber

explanation.surface: Someone tries to quash the comeback of a backer of a man called Murphy.
explanation.walkthrough: Murphy looks like a surname, but it is the old Irish-flavoured slang for a potato; the potato is a tuber.
explanation.definitionFit: To rebut a charge or argument is to refute it, putting it down as you would quash it.

clue.text: Ancient cattle commemorated in gold and jewels, say

parts.note: AU is the chemical symbol for gold

indicators.note: say asks for a word as spoken rather than as written

parts.note: rocks is slang for jewels, especially diamonds

explanation.surface: Prehistoric cattle are honoured with a memorial of gold and gems.
explanation.walkthrough: AU plus a sound-alike for rocks gives AUROCHS, the spelling with CH pronounced like K.
explanation.definitionFit: The aurochs was the wild ox of Europe, ancestor of domestic cattle, extinct since the seventeenth century.

clue.text: Undertaking a risk

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an enterprise or project taken on
second meaning: a hazard or gamble ...

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one phrase, a verb taking a risk, but splits into two nouns.
explanation.definitionFit: A venture is a business enterprise, and also a speculative stake where something may be lost.

clue.text: Bugle call gets one in for carpeting

indicators.note: gets ... in means the first item receives the second inside it

parts.note: taps is the bugle call sounded at lights out or at a military funeral
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A bugle summons someone in for a telling-off, carpeting meaning a reprimand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpeting' suggests a dressing-down, but here it means floor covering; TAPS takes in I.
explanation.definitionFit: Tapis is an old word, from French, for tapestry or a table or floor covering, as in 'on the tapis'.

clue.text: Pooh heard to encourage this kind of riding

indicators.note: heard asks for the word's sound, not its spelling

parts.note: Winnie-the-Pooh is the bear of A. A. Milne's stories
to back someone is to support and encourage them

explanation.surface: The voice of Winnie-the-Pooh is urging a style of horse riding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heard' governs only Pooh, the bear; the encouraging word follows in its normal spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Bareback riding is riding a horse without a saddle.

clue.text: City sailors tip these into the water

parts.note: Bath is a city in Somerset, England
an old salt is an experienced sailor

explanation.surface: Sailors from a city dump things over the side into the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The water is bath water: the whole clue describes what the answer is for.
explanation.definitionFit: Bath salts are scented crystals that people pour into a bath to soften or perfume the water.

clue.text: Familiar old man was an excellent parent

parts.note: grand means splendid or excellent
dad is a father

explanation.surface: A well-known elderly man had been a wonderful father.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Familiar' means informal: granddad is the casual word for a grandfather, or for any old man.
explanation.definitionFit: Granddad is an informal, friendly form of address for an elderly man.

clue.text: Manoeuvres of English archers revealed in systematic investigation

indicators.note: manoeuvres move troops into new positions, so the letters are redeployed

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
taken as written

explanation.surface: A careful study uncovers the drills of English bowmen.
explanation.definitionFit: Research is methodical study undertaken to discover facts or reach new conclusions.

clue.text: Eastern medicine protecting smug gourmet

indicators.note: to protect something is to shield it, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for eastern
a cure is a medicine or remedy
pi is short for pious, sanctimonious or smug

explanation.surface: An Eastern remedy is guarding a self-satisfied food lover.
explanation.walkthrough: Smug as a two-letter crossword stock word comes from pious, meaning sanctimonious.
explanation.definitionFit: An epicure is a person who takes particular pleasure in fine food and drink.

clue.text: Drawer in loom

definitions.meaning: first meaning: one who tows, as a drawer is one who draws or pulls
second meaning: to rise high and dominate, a verb

explanation.surface: A drawer has been left inside a weaving loom.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words are misread: the drawer pulls things, the 'tow-er', and loom is the verb, not the weaving frame.
explanation.definitionFit: To tower is to loom over something; a tower can also be read as one that tows a load.

clue.text: Scheme about river producing noisy argument

indicators.note: about means going round, so the first piece wraps around the second

parts.note: to wangle is to obtain by scheming or contrivance
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A plan concerning a river causes a loud row.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrangle is a long, angry dispute or quarrel.

clue.text: Put weight on, causing emotional strain

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to emphasise, lay importance on
second meaning: mental pressure or tension

explanation.surface: Gaining weight leads to anxiety.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put weight on' suggests getting fatter, but it means give emphasis.
explanation.definitionFit: To stress a point is to emphasise it, and stress is also anxiety caused by pressure.

clue.text: Dehydrated? Try this mixture

indicators.note: a mixture stirs its ingredients together into a new combination

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A drinks advert: feeling dried out? Try this mixture.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also hints at the answer, since a thirsty person would try a drink mixture.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone thirsty is in need of fluid, as a dehydrated body is.

clue.text: Person of high social standing waves

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a fashionable toff, an old informal noun
second meaning: the rolling motion of the sea

explanation.surface: A grand person waves to the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waves' reads as a verb, greeting people; it is the noun for rolling sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A swell is an elegant, wealthy or upper-class person, and also a long sequence of unbroken ocean waves.

clue.text: Give food to bear

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to nourish and keep alive
second meaning: to support or carry a weight, or to suffer

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests feeding an animal at a zoo; 'bear' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To sustain is to keep a person going with nourishment, and also to hold up a load or endure a loss.

clue.text: Discharge top of class who's back into drugs

indicators.note: going back means this word is read from its last letter to its first
into means one part is put inside the other

parts.note: E is slang for an ecstasy tablet, so two make drugs
dux, Latin for leader, is the Scottish and Commonwealth term for the top pupil in a class

explanation.surface: A star pupil returns to drug-taking and is expelled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top of class' looks like an instruction to take a first letter, but it is the word DUX, which goes backwards inside E and E.
explanation.definitionFit: To exude is to ooze or give off a liquid or smell, a slow kind of discharge.

clue.text: Wild double in first of games was not forced

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective, 'not forced', while the clue phrase is a verb phrase

indicators.note: something wild is out of control, so the letters run loose into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: 'first of' keeps only the first letter of 'games'

parts.note: the opening letter of games

explanation.surface: A wild double in a sport's opening game was an unforced shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' reads like a placement word but is part of the letters to be shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Unobliged means under no compulsion or duty, the state of someone who was not made to act.

clue.text: Furtive and salty, the tears

indicators.note: tears is the verb, ripping things up so the pieces land in a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sheds salty tears in secret.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tears' wants to be the noun, drops from the eye; it is the verb meaning rips.
explanation.definitionFit: Stealthy and furtive both describe acting secretly so as not to be noticed.

clue.text: Climb announced in a despatch

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something announced is spoken out, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: to despatch something is to send it off

explanation.surface: A climb is reported in an official despatch, as from a mountaineering expedition.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken aloud, 'a send' is indistinguishable from the answer, ASCEND.
explanation.definitionFit: To ascend is to go up, as a climber goes up a slope.
